title: ESPN to give air time to Protect College Sports Act opponent ahead of vote
content:
After receiving backlash for allowing Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) to promote a college sports senate bill on “College GameDay” on Saturday, ESPN will feature one of the bill’s most vocal opponents on its airwaves Tuesday.

NAACP President and CEO Derrick Johnson will appear on the 6 p.m. ET edition of “SportsCenter.” The move comes after the NAACP posted in response to Cruz’s appearance Saturday, “We’d love to have (Johnson) join you in his home state of (Mississippi) next week to express why the Protect College Sports Act is dangerous to Black Athletes and the Black community.”

An ESPN source said an appearance on Saturday’s “College GameDay” before the LSU-Ole Miss game was discussed, but “the focus shifted to Tuesday’s ‘SportsCenter’ in order to have the conversation take place before the bill is up for vote in the Senate.”

Cruz is the co-author of the Protect College Sports Act, a bipartisan bill before the U.S. Senate that aims to address several disruptive issues in college sports. Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) is the co-sponsor. The bill, as currently written, would allow the NCAA a limited antitrust exemption to establish new rules on athlete eligibility, transfers and player compensation, as well as limiting conference realignment and a future super league. A key component is a revenue-sharing “hard cap” that would prohibit schools from paying their athletes more than $48.5 million combined per year.

Johnson was one of several opponents of the bill who appeared on a media call Monday, alongside Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), who said the bill “protects the billions of dollars that coaches and sports industry executives are making over the suppression of compensation for some of the most highly valued athletes in the world.”

The 171-page bill includes a section titled “HBCU SPORTS MEDIA AND CONNECTIVITY PROGRAM,” which would award grants to improve broadband, technology and media infrastructure. Colorado coach Deion Sanders touts the program in a TV ad for PCSA.

“What makes this bill so inadequate and in many ways offensive is the overture as if it’s going to do something special for Historically Black Colleges and Universities,” Johnson said Monday. “They deserve direct federal investment, not a political trade-off that shields powerful college sports institutions, while asking black athletes to surrender rights, leverage, and a voice in the billion-dollar industry.”

Senators originally attempted to get the bill to a vote in early August before Congress’ summer recess but ran into 11th-hour opposition, including from the Congressional Black Caucus. Cruz said at the time the authors had a “guarantee” for a vote upon returning this week. At a press conference Monday, he said, “In the next 10 days, the Senate is voting on the Protect College Sports Act.”

Later Monday, Cruz and Cantwell held a press conference in Washington, D.C. alongside several college coaches and athletes, including men’s basketball coaches Kelvin Sampson, Mark Few and John Calipari.

“(The bill) cracks down on fake NIL,” Cruz said. “It cracks down on a booster in a back alley with a bag of cash. And it ensures the system can remain competitive and fair.”
